pos: n. (the Pomerelian Cistercian abbey of 1276, now a cathedral, holding one of the surviving Gutenberg Bibles)
etymology: Polish Pelplin, from a local water or personal name; German Pelplin.
biblical_def: Pelplin in Pomerelia was founded in 1276 when Cistercians from Doberan were moved to the Wierzyca valley, and the brick church they raised is one of the largest of the order anywhere, with a nave of some two hundred and sixty feet and a set of carved stalls that survived every war since. Since 1824 it has been a cathedral. Its library holds a copy of the Gutenberg Bible, one of about four dozen surviving, carried out of the country and back again in the last war. The dictionary records Pelplin for that volume, because a printed Bible in a monastic library is the beginning of the end of a particular monopoly. What the press did was make the text available for the ordinary test, which is exactly what the law of the Lord is said to be able to bear, “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psa 19:7), and the reason it must be open is that it is given to reach the unlearned, “it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). The Berean habit requires a copy in the hand, “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11), and the household duty Moses laid down presumes the same, “thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” (Deu 6:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a Bible as the book containing the Scriptures; the press as a machine for printing; an incunabulum is a book from the infancy of printing; a cathedral as the principal church of a diocese; and a library as a collection of books.
webster_full: BIBLE, n. THE BOOK, by way of eminence; the sacred volume, in which are contained the revelations of God.
PRESS, n. An instrument or machine for pressing; a machine for printing, whence the art of printing.
TYPE, n. A printing letter; the metal letters used in printing; emblem; figure.
CATHEDRAL, n. The see or seat of a bishop; the principal church in a diocese.
LIBRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution.

The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
corruption_summary: Pomerelian Cistercian abbey of 1276, now a cathedral, whose library holds a Gutenberg Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an available Bible is the enemy of every monopoly on doctrine. Pelplin keeps a Gutenberg in a house that once chained its books, and the psalmist's claim for the text requires that it be read rather than guarded, “converting the soul” (Psa 19:7).

The live temptation is to treat such a volume as a treasure rather than as a tool, which is how monastic libraries kept the text and lost its use. Scripture insists on the opposite order: the entrance of the words is for the unlearned, “The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130); verification is the commended instinct, “they received the word with all readiness of mind” (Act 17:11); and teaching is laid on fathers at every hour of an ordinary day, “when thou walkest by the way” (Deu 6:7).

pos: n. (the Lesser Polish Cistercian abbey of 1140, the first of the order in Poland, burial place of the chronicler Wincenty Kadlubek)
etymology: Polish Jedrzejow, Andrew's place, from Jedrzej, Andrew; formerly Morimundus Minor.
biblical_def: Jedrzejow in Lesser Poland was founded in 1140 and settled from Morimond, which made it the first Cistercian house in Poland and the parent of the Polish branch of the order. Its second distinction is a man: Wincenty Kadlubek, bishop of Krakow, resigned his see in 1218, took the habit at Jedrzejow and died there, leaving the Chronica Polonorum, the earliest sustained narrative of the Polish past written by a Pole. The abbey kept his tomb and the chronicle kept the nation's memory. The dictionary records Jedrzejow for that office of remembering, which Scripture treats as a duty rather than an antiquarian taste. The psalmist makes handing on the record a refusal to be silent, “We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4), and the thing to be handed down is measured by its usefulness to those who come after, “that ye may tell it to the generation following” (Psa 48:13). A man who leaves a true account leaves an estate of a kind, “A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children” (Pro 13:22), and the contentment proper to such a portion is confessed and not merely felt, “yea, I have a goodly heritage” (Psa 16:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chronicle as a historical account in order of time; an annal as a year's record of events; an inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor; memory as the faculty of recollecting; and a monument as anything by which the memory of persons or events is preserved.
webster_full: CHRONICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
ANNALS, n. A species of history digested in order of time, or a relation of events in chronological order.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession or in course of law.
MEMORY, n. The faculty of the mind by which it retains the knowledge of past events.
MONUMENT, n. Any thing by which the memory of a person or of an event is preserved or perpetuated.

corruption_summary: Poland's first Cistercian house, 1140, settled from Morimond, burial place of the chronicler Wincenty Kadlubek.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that keeping a true record is a duty laid on the living. Kadlubek resigned a bishopric and spent his last years writing his people's history, and the psalmist frames that labour as a refusal rather than a hobby, “We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4).

The live temptation is to write the past to flatter the house that pays for the ink, which medieval chronicles did constantly and Kadlubek did sometimes. The corrective is the stated audience: a record is made “that ye may tell it to the generation following” (Psa 48:13). An honest account is itself a bequest, “A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children” (Pro 13:22), and the right response to receiving one is gratitude, “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places” (Psa 16:6).

pos: n. (the Lesser Polish Cistercian abbey of 1179, keeping one of the best-preserved Romanesque chapter houses in Europe)
etymology: Polish Wachock, from a local personal name; latinised Vonchoczk.
biblical_def: Wachock in the Holy Cross mountains was founded in 1179 by Bishop Gedeon of Krakow and settled from Morimond. Its distinction is its chapter house: a square Romanesque room with four bays springing from a single central pillar, built of banded grey and yellow sandstone, almost untouched since the twelfth century and among the finest surviving anywhere. That room is where the community met daily to read the rule, confess faults and decide business. The dictionary records Wachock for what a chapter house was for, and for the wisdom it was meant to practise. Deliberation among brethren is good, but Scripture will not let counsel rest in the counsellors, “Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding” (Pro 3:5). Understanding itself is defined by obedience rather than by acuteness, “a good understanding have all they that do his commandments” (Psa 111:10). The standing danger of any assembly of able men is named without softening, “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Pro 16:18), and the grace that meets the opposite disposition is promised in the same terms, “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” (Jam 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chapter as an assembly of the clergy of a cathedral or of a religious house; counsel as advice, deliberation; a pillar as a column, a supporter; humility as freedom from pride; and a rule as a prescribed form of conduct.
webster_full: CHAPTER, n. An assembly of the clergy of a cathedral or collegiate church; also, a meeting of a religious order.
COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request; deliberation; consultation.
PILLAR, n. A kind of irregular column, round and insulated; a supporter; that which sustains.
HUMILITY, n. In ethics, freedom from pride and arrogance; a modest estimate of one's own worth.
RULE, n. Government; sway; empire; also, a prescribed form or standard of conduct or practice.

The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endureth for ever.

Jam 4:6
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
corruption_summary: Lesser Polish Cistercian house of 1179 with a Romanesque chapter house almost untouched since the twelfth century.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an assembly of able men still has to distrust itself. Wachock's chapter met daily under a single pillar to read the rule before doing business, and the proverb that should govern every such room forbids leaning on the room, “lean not unto thine own understanding” (Pro 3:5).

The live temptation is a competence that mistakes itself for wisdom. Scripture defines understanding by what a man does rather than by what he can argue, “a good understanding have all they that do his commandments” (Psa 111:10); it names the sequence from pride to ruin without qualification, “Pride goeth before destruction” (Pro 16:18); and it fixes the direction in which grace runs, “but giveth grace unto the humble” (Jam 4:6).

pos: n. (the Lesser Polish Cistercian abbey of 1185, settled from Morimond, keeping a Romanesque church and chapter house)
etymology: Polish koprzywa, a nettle, so the nettle place.
biblical_def: Koprzywnica on the Vistula was founded in 1185 by the palatine Nicholas of Bogoria and settled from Morimond. Its name is taken from the nettle, a weed of waste ground, and the siting is typical of the order: a river valley nobody wanted, taken because nobody wanted it. The Romanesque church and chapter house survive, with a baroque front added later. The dictionary records Koprzywnica for the figure its own name supplies. The Cistercians prized the fruitfulness of a cleared valley and spoke of their houses as vineyards, and the gospel keeps the figure but moves the root of the fruit out of the ground entirely, “He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit” (Joh 15:5). The psalmist's blessed man is planted rather than self-rooted, “like a tree planted by the rivers of water” (Psa 1:3), and the prophet sets the same tree against drought to show what its roots are reaching, “that spreadeth out her roots by the river” (Jer 17:8). The water itself is not the monastery's stream but the city of God's, “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God” (Psa 46:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a nettle as a stinging plant; fruit as the produce of a tree or plant; a vineyard as a plantation of vines; to graft as to insert a shoot into another stock; and a root as that part of a plant which enters the earth.
webster_full: NETTLE, n. A plant of the genus Urtica, whose prickles fret the skin and cause acute pain.
FRUIT, n. In a general sense, whatever the earth produces for the nourishment of animals; the produce of a tree or plant.
VINEYARD, n. A plantation of vines producing grapes; an inclosure or field devoted to the culture of grapes.
GRAFT, v.t. To insert a shoot or scion of one tree or plant into another for propagation.
ROOT, n. That part of a plant which enters and fixes itself in the earth, and serves to support and nourish it.

I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
Psa 1:3
And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.

For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
Psa 46:4
There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High.
corruption_summary: Lesser Polish Cistercian house of 1185 in a nettle valley on the Vistula, settled from Morimond.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that fruit comes from union and not from husbandry. Koprzywnica was planted in a nettle valley and made it yield, honest work of a kind the order excelled at, and the Lord's own figure moves the source of the fruit off the land altogether, “for without me ye can do nothing” (Joh 15:5).

The live temptation is to read a flourishing institution as evidence of a flourishing soul. Scripture keeps the tree passive in the decisive respect: it is “planted by the rivers of water” (Psa 1:3) and does not plant itself; its roots are described as reaching toward a supply it did not dig, “and shall not see when heat cometh” (Jer 17:8); and the river that gladdens the city belongs to the city's God, “the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High” (Psa 46:4).

pos: n. (the Lesser Polish Cistercian abbey of 1176, fortified with walls and towers against Tatar and Teutonic raids)
biblical_def: Sulejow on the Pilica was founded in 1176 by Casimir the Just and settled from Morimond, and it is the most thoroughly fortified Cistercian house in Poland: a circuit of stone wall with six towers and a gate, thrown round the abbey after Tatar raids and kept up through the wars with the Teutonic Order. The Romanesque church stands with its original portal. The dictionary records Sulejow because a walled monastery raises the question of what Christians are to make of walls. Scripture is not squeamish about them: the psalmist invites a deliberate survey of Jerusalem's defences, “Walk about Zion, and go round about her: tell the towers thereof” (Psa 48:12), and Nehemiah's wall is built with enthusiasm and reported with satisfaction, “So built we the wall” (Neh 4:6). But the security promised is attached to a tent rather than to masonry, “a tabernacle that shall not be taken down” (Isa 33:20), and the city finally in view is one that comes down rather than one that is thrown up, “I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven” (Rev 21:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bulwark as a fortification, a rampart; a tower as a lofty building; a rampart as an elevation of earth round a place; a fortress as a fortified place; and a tabernacle as a tent, a temporary habitation.
webster_full: BULWARK, n. In fortification, a bastion, or a rampart; a mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting cannon shot.
TOWER, n. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation and consisting of several stories.
RAMPART, n. In fortification, an elevation or mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting the cannon of an enemy.
FORTRESS, n. A fortified place; a place of defense; a fort; a castle.
TABERNACLE, n. A tent; a temporary habitation; among the Israelites, a movable building for worship.
scriptures: Walk about Zion, and go round about her: tell the towers thereof.
Neh 4:6

Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities: thine eyes shall see Jerusalem a quiet habitation, a tabernacle that shall not be taken down; not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed, neither shall any of the cords thereof be broken.
Rev 21:2
And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
corruption_summary: Lesser Polish Cistercian house of 1176 walled with six towers against Tatar and Teutonic raids.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that defences are lawful and not final. Sulejow walled itself after the Tatars came, and the psalmist's own instruction is to go and count such towers rather than to despise them, “tell the towers thereof” (Psa 48:12).

The live temptation is to let the wall become the hope, which is the standing disease of an institution that has been attacked. Nehemiah builds and says so plainly, “for the people had a mind to work” (Neh 4:6); but the immovable thing in Isaiah's picture is a tent and not a bastion, “not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed” (Isa 33:20); and the city that lasts is received rather than constructed, “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev 21:2).

pos: n. (the Silesian Cistercian abbey of 1227, whose Book of Henrykow preserves the earliest recorded sentence in Polish)
etymology: Polish Henrykow, Henry's place, for Duke Henry the Bearded; German Heinrichau.
biblical_def: Henrykow in Silesia was founded in 1227 by the notary Nicholas with the support of Duke Henry the Bearded, and settled from Lubiaz. Its fame rests on a manuscript. The Liber fundationis, the Book of Henrykow, was begun about 1270 as a record of the abbey's estates and the disputes over them, and in the middle of its Latin an abbot set down what a Bohemian settler said to his wife at the millstone, in her own tongue: the earliest sentence in Polish anywhere in writing. A land register preserved a language. The dictionary records Henrykow for that accident, because it is the vernacular principle arriving early and by the back door. Scripture claims to be light precisely where it enters an untaught mind, “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130), and the instrument of sanctifying is a word that must therefore be understood, “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth” (Joh 17:17). The teacher's stock is knowledge others may come and get, “they should seek the law at his mouth” (Mal 2:7), and every claim is to be taken back to a written standard, “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the vernacular as belonging to the country of one's birth; a cartulary is a register of a monastery's charters; a charter as a written instrument of grant; a quern is a hand-mill; and a tongue as a language.

CARTULARY, n. A register book, as of a monastery; a place where papers or records are kept.
CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant or contract.
QUERN, n. A hand-mill for grinding grain; a simple instrument consisting of two stones.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; speech; a language.

For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.

To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Silesian Cistercian abbey of 1227 whose estate register preserves the earliest written sentence in Polish.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the plain tongue is not a concession but the point. Henrykow's abbot wrote a settler's Polish into a Latin register almost by accident, and the psalmist had already made plainness the text's own claim, “it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130).

The live temptation is the one the medieval church institutionalised, a sacred language kept from the people it was meant to reach. Scripture ties sanctification to a word that must be understood to work, “thy word is truth” (Joh 17:17); it makes the minister a source others may come and draw from, “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7); and it submits every claim to a written test any reader can apply, “if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

pos: n. (the Silesian Cistercian abbey of 1175, the largest of the order in Silesia, immense in its baroque rebuilding and now largely empty)
etymology: Polish Lubiaz, from a Slavic root for a loved or pleasant place; German Leubus.
biblical_def: Lubiaz on the Oder was settled in 1175 from Pforta and became the oldest and greatest Cistercian house in Silesia, mother of Henrykow, Kamieniec and Krzeszow. Between 1681 and 1739 it was rebuilt on a scale that beggars description: a facade some six hundred feet long, a prince's hall painted by Willmann, refectories and libraries fit for a court. It was secularised in 1810, used as a military hospital, a stud and a wartime factory, and stands today largely empty, its frescoes peeling behind scaffolding. The dictionary records Lubiaz as the plainest monument in central Europe to building for one's own name. Nebuchadnezzar's sentence on his own capital is the exact register of a six-hundred-foot monastic facade, “Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power” (Dan 4:30), and the day appointed against such height is announced in advance, “upon every one that is proud and lofty” (Isa 2:12). Laodicea supplies the self-assessment that goes with it, “I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing” (Rev 3:17), and the blessing is pronounced on the exact opposite condition, “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines baroque in the sense of grotesque or irregular; magnificence as grandeur of appearance; a facade as the front of a building; pride as inordinate self-esteem; and to secularize as to convert to common use.
webster_full: MAGNIFICENCE, n. Grandeur of appearance; greatness and splendor of show or state.
FACADE, n. The front of a building, especially the principal front.
PRIDE, n. Inordinate self-esteem; an unreasonable conceit of one's own superiority.
SUMPTUOUS, adj. Costly; expensive; hence, splendid; magnificent.
SECULARIZE, v.t. To convert from spiritual or ecclesiastical appropriation to secular or common use.
scriptures: Dan 4:30
The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?
Isa 2:12
For the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up; and he shall be brought low:
Rev 3:17
Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:
Mat 5:3
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: Silesia's oldest and greatest Cistercian house, 1175, rebuilt on a princely scale and now largely empty.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an order founded on austerity can end in a six-hundred-foot facade, and that the slide is a matter of the heart rather than of architecture. Nebuchadnezzar's boast over his own capital is the register the building speaks in, “for the honour of my majesty” (Dan 4:30).

The live temptation is to admire the fabric and forget the appetite that raised it, or to despise the fabric and congratulate ourselves on a cheaper vanity. Scripture addresses the appetite: a day is appointed “upon every one that is lifted up” (Isa 2:12); a rich church is the likeliest to misjudge itself, “Because thou sayest, I am rich” (Rev 3:17); and the kingdom is assigned to a condition no endowment can purchase, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Mat 5:3).

pos: n. (the Silesian Cistercian nunnery of 1202, the first women's house of the order in Silesia, burial place of Hedwig of Silesia)
etymology: Polish Trzebnica, from trzebic, to clear ground; German Trebnitz.
biblical_def: Trzebnica in Silesia was founded in 1202 by Duke Henry the Bearded at the urging of his wife Hedwig, and was the first Cistercian house for women in Silesia. Hedwig retired there after Henry's death, died in 1243, and was canonised in 1267; her tomb in the abbey church became one of the great pilgrimage goals of central Europe, and the house was rebuilt in baroque splendour around it. Her charity was real: she founded hospitals, fed the poor in famine and buried the dead after the Mongol defeat at Legnica. The dictionary honours the charity and names the cult that grew over it. A shrine that directs petitions to a dead woman trespasses on an office Scripture assigns to one Person only, “there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5), and the intercession actually offered is continuous and needs no supplement, “he ever liveth to make intercession for them” (Heb 7:25). The Christian is not thereby shut out of the court but invited into it, and the invitation is addressed to every believer without an intermediary, “that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need” (Heb 4:16). Nor is the advocate's place vacant or distant; He holds it at the seat of authority and pleads there continually, “It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again” (Rom 8:34). Hedwig may be honoured as a believer who fed the hungry. She may not be addressed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines canonization as the act of declaring a person a saint; a saint in Scripture as a person sanctified, a believer; intercession as prayer or solicitation in favor of another; a shrine as a case for sacred things; and invocation as the act of calling upon in prayer.
webster_full: CANONIZATION, n. The act of declaring a man a saint, or rather of ranking a deceased person in the catalogue of saints.
SAINT, n. A person sanctified; a holy or godly person; in Scripture, one who is renewed in heart.
INTERCESSION, n. Prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another; mediation.
SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle, in which sacred things are deposited; a tomb or altar.
INVOCATION, n. The act of addressing in prayer; the form or act of calling for the assistance or presence of any being.
scriptures: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
Heb 7:25
Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
Rom 8:34
Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us.
Heb 4:16
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
corruption_summary: Silesia's first Cistercian nunnery, 1202, and the shrine of Hedwig, whose real charity became a pilgrimage cult.
corruption_paragraphs: Hedwig of Silesia deserves the historical honour. She founded hospitals, fed the hungry through famine and buried the dead after Legnica, and the dictionary does not grudge her a word of it. What followed her death is another matter. Canonised in 1267, she became an object of invocation, and Trzebnica was rebuilt around her tomb to receive petitioners. That traffic crosses a line Scripture draws in a single clause: “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5).

The corruption is not a medieval relic. Rome still teaches the invocation of saints, and defends it as asking a friend to pray rather than as worship; the objection is not to friendship but to the office, since the intercession on offer is already unbroken, “seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them” (Heb 7:25), and already occupied by One at the place of authority, “who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us” (Rom 8:34). The access that follows is direct and invited, which leaves no need for an intermediary court, “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace” (Heb 4:16).
roots_summary: Greek mesites (G3316), a mediator, a go-between; Greek entugchano (G1793), to intercede; Greek pantote (G3842), always; Greek parrhesia (G3954), boldness, freedom of access.
roots_lines: Greek mesites (G3316) — a mediator, one who goes between; “one mediator between God and men”, 1 Timothy 2:5.
Greek entugchano (G1793) — to plead with, to intercede for; “to make intercession for them”, Hebrews 7:25.
Greek pantelos (G3838) — completely, to the uttermost; “able also to save them to the uttermost”, Hebrews 7:25.
Greek katakrino (G2632) — to condemn, to give sentence against; “Who is he that condemneth?”, Romans 8:34.
Greek parrhesia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of access; “come boldly unto the throne of grace”, Hebrews 4:16.
usage: “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5) — the clause the shrine crosses.
“he ever liveth to make intercession for them” (Heb 7:25) — an intercession needing no supplement.
“come boldly unto the throne of grace” (Heb 4:16) — access that leaves no intermediary court.

pos: n. (the Silesian Cistercian abbey of 1247, settled from Lubiaz, a landed house of granges and mills)
etymology: Polish kamien, a stone, so the stony place; German Kamenz.
biblical_def: Kamieniec in Silesia, properly Kamieniec Zabkowicki, was settled in 1247 from Lubiaz after an earlier house of canons there failed, and it grew into a substantial landed abbey holding villages, granges, mills and fishponds along the Nysa. The church was rebuilt in brick Gothic with a baroque interior, and after the secularisation of 1810 the estate passed to the Prussian royal house, which built a vast neo-Gothic palace on the hill above. The dictionary records Kamieniec for the plain business of estate management, which occupied far more monastic hours than contemplation did, and which Scripture treats as a spiritual matter rather than a secular one. One thing only is asked of a man handling what is not his own, “it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2), and the Lord makes small accounts the assay of great ones, “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luk 16:10). The commendation at the end names fidelity and not yield, “thou hast been faithful over a few things” (Mat 25:21), and the proverb insists that a man actually know the state of what he keeps, “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks” (Pro 27:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a steward as one entrusted with the management of another's affairs; a grange as a farm with its buildings; a bailiff as an officer who manages an estate; an account as a reckoning; and diligent as steadily applied, industrious.
webster_full: STEWARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns, superintend the other servants, and collect the rents.
GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings, stables, &c.; a farm-house with the barns and other buildings.
BAILIFF, n. An officer appointed to manage an estate, collect rents and direct husbandry.
ACCOUNT, n. A computation or reckoning; a registry of debts and credits; also, a reason or explanation.
DILIGENT, adj. Steady in application to business; constant in effort to accomplish what is undertaken.
scriptures: Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds.
corruption_summary: Silesian Cistercian abbey of 1247 with villages, granges and mills on the Nysa, secularised in 1810.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that estate management is a spiritual office. Kamieniec's monks spent more hours on rents and fishponds than on contemplation, and the apostolic requirement over every such hour is single, “that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).

The live temptation is the division that treats accounts as secular and prayer as spiritual, so that a cellarer need only be competent. Christ will not have the division: small sums test large ones, “he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much” (Luk 16:10); the commendation at the reckoning names fidelity rather than return, “Well done, thou good and faithful servant” (Mat 25:21); and the proverb requires real knowledge of what is held in trust, “and look well to thy herds” (Pro 27:23).

pos: n. (the Silesian abbey of 1242, Benedictine then Cistercian, a baroque pilgrimage house built round a Marian image)
etymology: Polish Krzeszow, from a Slavic personal name; German Gruessau.
biblical_def: Krzeszow in the Sudeten foothills was founded in 1242 as a Benedictine house by Anne of Bohemia, passed to the Cistercians of Lubiaz in 1292, and between 1728 and 1735 was rebuilt as one of the most ambitious baroque churches in central Europe, with a facade of twin towers, frescoes by Neunhertz and the Silesian dukes' mausoleum attached. The whole design converges on a thirteenth-century painted panel of the Virgin above the high altar, the object the pilgrims came for, and the complex remains a Marian pilgrimage goal. The dictionary records Krzeszow as the clearest architectural statement of a corruption: a building ordered around an image. The second commandment forbids the making of such objects for worship in terms that admit no exception for sincerity or artistry, “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4), and the LORD assigns the reason to His own jealousy for glory, “my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8). The psalmist's mockery of such objects is directed at their manufacture rather than at the sincerity of those who kneel, “the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4), and the apostle's closing charge to his own congregation is flat and without qualification, “keep yourselves from idols” (1Jo 5:21). The baroque is not the offence; a panel addressed in prayer is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an image as a representation of any person or thing; an idol as an image or representation worshipped as a god; idolatry as the worship of idols or images; a pilgrimage as a journey to a holy place; and veneration as the highest degree of respect.
webster_full: IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
IDOLATRY, n. The worship of idols, images, or any thing made by hands, or which is not God.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A long journey, particularly a journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable.
VENERATION, n. The highest degree of respect and reverence; respect mingled with some degree of awe.
scriptures: Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Isa 42:8
I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen.
corruption_summary: Silesian abbey of 1242 rebuilt in baroque splendour around a thirteenth-century Marian image, still a pilgrimage goal.
corruption_paragraphs: Krzeszow's architecture is an argument. Twin towers, a painted vault and a mausoleum all converge on a small medieval panel of the Virgin, because that panel is what the pilgrims came to address. The second commandment speaks to exactly this, and it legislates against the making and not merely against the mistaking, “or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4).

Rome distinguishes the honour paid to an image from the worship due to God and answers the objection with that distinction. Scripture answers the distinction. The LORD grounds the prohibition in His own refusal to share, “I am the LORD: that is my name” (Isa 42:8); the psalmist mocks the manufacture itself, “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4); and John's last word to his children is not a nuance but a command, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1Jo 5:21).
roots_summary: Hebrew pesel (H6459), a graven image; Hebrew temunah (H8544), a likeness; Hebrew atsab (H6091), an idol; Greek eidolon (G1497), an image, an idol.
roots_lines: Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image, a carved idol; “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image”, Exodus 20:4.
Hebrew temunah (H8544) — a likeness, a form; “or any likeness of any thing”, Exodus 20:4.
Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, weight, honour; “and my glory will I not give to another”, Isaiah 42:8.
Hebrew atsab (H6091) — an idol, a thing fashioned; “Their idols are silver and gold”, Psalm 115:4.
Greek eidolon (G1497) — an image, an idol; “keep yourselves from idols”, 1 John 5:21.
usage: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) — the command is against the making.
“neither my praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8) — the LORD's own stated reason.
“Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1Jo 5:21) — John's last word, not a nuance.
